lead: Three measurable coefficients describe how the volume of a substance responds to heat and pressure: the volume expansivity β, the isothermal compressibility κT and the isentropic compressibility κs. With the TdS equations they give the Mayer relation, cp − cv = Tvβ²/κT, which yields cv of a liquid, where it cannot be measured directly. The same slopes give the Joule-Thomson coefficient, which says whether a gas cools or warms in a throttle.
prereq: You need: the cyclic relation from Exact differentials, reciprocity and cyclic relations, and the TdS equations and the enthalpy relation from Maxwell relations.

blocks.where: β is the volume expansivity (coefficient of volume expansion), in 1/K: the fractional increase of volume per kelvin at constant pressure.

κ<sub>T</sub> is the isothermal compressibility, in 1/Pa: the fractional decrease of volume per pascal at constant temperature. The minus sign makes it positive. Its inverse is the isothermal bulk modulus.
κ<sub>s</sub> is the isentropic (adiabatic) compressibility; it sets the speed of sound, c = √(v/κ<sub>s</sub>).

blocks.text: For an ideal gas, v = RT/p gives β = 1/T, κ<sub>T</sub> = 1/p and κ<sub>s</sub> = 1/(γp), where γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub>. At 300 K and 100 kPa, β = 0.00333 K⁻¹ and κ<sub>T</sub> = 0.01 kPa⁻¹. Liquids are far stiffer: for water at 25 °C, β ≈ 2.57 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ and κ<sub>T</sub> ≈ 4.52 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹.

The cyclic relation links the two coefficients to the pressure slope: (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> = −(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>/(∂v/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = β/κ<sub>T</sub>. For water this is about 5.7 × 10⁵ Pa/K, nearly 6 bar for each kelvin, which is why a completely full, sealed vessel of liquid must never be heated.

sections.h3: The Mayer relation for c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub>

items: Take the two TdS equations: T ds = c<sub>v</sub>dT + T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>dv and T ds = c<sub>p</sub>dT − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>dp.
Hold v fixed (dv = 0): c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>.
Replace (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> by the cyclic relation: c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = −T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>²(∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub>.
Write the slopes with β and κ<sub>T</sub>: (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = vβ and (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = −1/(vκ<sub>T</sub>).

blocks.text: With T in K, v in m³/kg, β in 1/K and κ<sub>T</sub> in 1/Pa, the result is in J/(kg·K).

items: κ<sub>T</sub> is positive for every stable substance and β² cannot be negative, so c<sub>p</sub> ≥ c<sub>v</sub> always.
c<sub>p</sub> = c<sub>v</sub> where β = 0, as for water at about 4 °C, its density maximum.
For an ideal gas Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub> = T(RT/p)(1/T²)(p) = R, so c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R. Many textbooks call this ideal-gas form Mayer's relation.
Dividing the two TdS equations at constant s gives the ratio γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> = κ<sub>T</sub>/κ<sub>s</sub>.

blocks.text: A throttle (a valve or porous plug) is adiabatic, does no work and leaves the kinetic energy nearly unchanged, so h₁ = h₂: throttling is a constant-enthalpy process. The Joule-Thomson coefficient (some syllabi say Joule-Kelvin) is the temperature change per unit pressure change at constant enthalpy:

blocks.where: μ<sub>JT</sub> is in K/Pa, or K/bar in practice. Since pressure falls in a throttle, μ<sub>JT</sub> > 0 means the gas cools.

blocks.text: Set dh = 0 in dh = c<sub>p</sub>dT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>]dp and solve for dT/dp:
c<sub>p</sub> is the specific heat at constant pressure; v is the specific volume.

For an ideal gas Tβ = 1, so μJT = 0: throttling changes its pressure but not its temperature. A real gas cools when Tβ > 1 and warms when Tβ < 1. The states with μJT = 0 form the inversion curve, and its highest temperature is the maximum inversion temperature. Nitrogen and air have it far above room temperature, so they cool in a throttle; hydrogen and helium have it far below, so they must be precooled before throttling can cool them.

At low pressure a van der Waals gas gives μ<sub>JT</sub> ≈ (2a/RT − b)/c<sub>p,m</sub> per mole, which is zero at the inversion temperature T<sub>i</sub> = 2a/(Rb). It shows the mechanism, attraction (a) against molecular size (b), but overshoots measured values. Figure 4.7.1 plots it for nitrogen.

examples.question: For liquid water at 25 °C (298.15 K), v = 0.001003 m³/kg, β = 2.57 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, κ<sub>T</sub> = 4.52 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹ and c<sub>p</sub> = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K). Find c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub>, c<sub>v</sub> and γ, and the pressure rise per kelvin if the water is heated in a full, rigid, sealed vessel.
steps: Rigid vessel: (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> = β/κ<sub>T</sub> = 2.57 × 10⁻⁴/4.52 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 5.69 × 10⁵ Pa/K, about 5.7 bar per kelvin.
examples.answer: c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = 0.0437 kJ/(kg·K), about 1 % of c<sub>p</sub>; c<sub>v</sub> = 4.136 kJ/(kg·K); γ = 1.011; the sealed vessel gains about 5.7 bar per kelvin.

examples.question: Nitrogen at 300 K is throttled from 20 bar to 1 bar. Estimate its temperature change with the low-pressure van der Waals result μ<sub>JT</sub> ≈ (2a/RT − b)/c<sub>p,m</sub>, taking a = 0.137 Pa·m⁶/mol², b = 3.87 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol, c<sub>p,m</sub> = 29.1 J/(mol·K) and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Also estimate the inversion temperature.
steps: ΔT ≈ μ<sub>JT</sub>Δp = 0.2445 × (1 − 20) = −4.6 K, so the gas leaves at about 295.4 K.
Inversion temperature: T<sub>i</sub> = 2a/(Rb) = 0.274/(8.314 × 3.87 × 10⁻⁵) = 0.274/(3.218 × 10⁻⁴) = 852 K. At 300 K nitrogen is far below it, so μ<sub>JT</sub> is positive and it cools.
examples.answer: μ<sub>JT</sub> ≈ 0.245 K/bar, so the nitrogen cools by about 4.6 K, to about 295.4 K. The van der Waals inversion temperature is about 852 K; the measured maximum is lower, near 620 K.

traps: Dropping the minus sign in κ<sub>T</sub>. (∂v/∂p)<sub>T</sub> is negative, and κ<sub>T</sub> must come out positive.
Mixing units in Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub>. With κ<sub>T</sub> in 1/Pa the answer is in J/(kg·K); with κ<sub>T</sub> in 1/bar it is 10⁵ times too small.
Saying throttling always cools a gas. It cools only below the inversion temperature (μ<sub>JT</sub> > 0); an ideal gas does not change temperature at all.
Confusing μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T/∂p)<sub>h</sub> with (∂T/∂p)<sub>s</sub>. Throttling is at constant enthalpy, not constant entropy.

quiz.q: Define the volume expansivity and the isothermal compressibility, with units.
Write the general Mayer relation and the Joule-Thomson coefficient.
Why is c<sub>p</sub> never smaller than c<sub>v</sub>?
quiz.a: In c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub>, T and v are positive, β² cannot be negative and κ<sub>T</sub> is positive for any stable substance, so the difference is zero or positive.

quiz.q: Why can throttling cool a real gas but not an ideal gas?
quiz.a: μ<sub>JT</sub> = v(Tβ − 1)/c<sub>p</sub>. For an ideal gas Tβ = 1, so μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0. A real gas below its inversion temperature has Tβ > 1, so μ<sub>JT</sub> > 0 and it cools as its pressure falls.

quiz.q: Show that β = 1/T and κ<sub>T</sub> = 1/p for an ideal gas, and find c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> for air.
quiz.a: v = RT/p: (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = R/p = v/T, so β = 1/T; (∂v/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −RT/p² = −v/p, so κ<sub>T</sub> = 1/p. Then Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub> = pv/T = R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K).

quiz.q: With van der Waals constants a = 0.00346 Pa·m⁶/mol² and b = 2.38 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol for helium, estimate its inversion temperature. Can throttling at room temperature cool helium?
quiz.a: T<sub>i</sub> = 2a/(Rb) = 0.00692/(8.314 × 2.38 × 10⁻⁵) = 35 K. Room temperature is far above it, so μ<sub>JT</sub> < 0 and helium warms in a throttle; it must be precooled first.

quiz.q: Find c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> and the sign of μ<sub>JT</sub> for liquid water at its density maximum near 4 °C.
quiz.a: There β = 0, so c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = Tvβ²/κ<sub>T</sub> = 0: c<sub>p</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>. And μ<sub>JT</sub> = v(0 − 1)/c<sub>p</sub> = −v/c<sub>p</sub>, negative, so liquid water warms slightly when throttled.

beyond: The Linde-Hampson cycle liquefies air by throttling it after compression and counter-flow precooling, and the same principle runs cryocoolers for infrared sensors. Speed-of-sound measurement gives κ<sub>s</sub>, and with the Mayer relation it gives c<sub>v</sub> of fluids at high pressure. Search next: Linde-Hampson cycle, Joule-Thomson inversion curve, speed of sound and compressibility.

figure.caption: The low-pressure van der Waals estimate of the Joule-Thomson coefficient of nitrogen: 0.245 K/bar at 300 K, so throttling from 20 bar to 1 bar cools the gas by about 4.6 K; the coefficient falls with temperature and changes sign at the estimated inversion temperature of 852 K.
